home.title: Current Conditions
home.subtitle: Solar wind parameters and geomagnetic indices, updated continuously from the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center.

solarWind.title: Solar Wind
solarWind.subtitle: Plasma and interplanetary magnetic field measured at L1, one minute apart.

about.title: About the solar wind
about.body: The solar wind is a continuous stream of charged particles (plasma) emitted by the Sun's atmosphere. When this stream reaches Earth, it transfers energy into the magnetosphere. It has two components: the properties of the plasma (speed, density, temperature) and those of the embedded magnetic field, the Interplanetary Magnetic Field. Geomagnetic storms are typically triggered by high-speed solar wind combined with a strong southward IMF — storm intensity increases as the Bz value becomes more negative.

geomagIndices.title: Geomagnetic Indices
geomagIndices.subtitle: How strongly Earth's magnetic field is currently being disturbed.

about.title: About the Dst index
about.body: The Disturbance Storm Time index measures geomagnetic storm severity in nanoTeslas, from the average horizontal magnetic field at four near-equatorial observatories, hourly. It tracks the growth and recovery of the ring current in Earth's magnetosphere — the lower the value, the more energy is stored there. Below −50 nT indicates a moderate storm, below −100 nT a severe one. The chart compares observations against the model's predictions.

about.title: About the Kp index
about.body: The Kp index is a geomagnetic activity index derived from magnetometers around the world, measured every three hours. It is quasi-logarithmic from 0 to 9, where 5 indicates a moderate storm, 7 a severe storm, and 9 an extreme storm.

solarActivity.title: Solar Activity
solarActivity.subtitle: The Sun's current face, and where we sit in its 11-year cycle.

about.title: About the solar cycle
about.body: The Sun follows a periodic 11-year cycle driven by its internal magnetic field, which completely flips orientation once per decade. The progression is most visibly tracked by sunspot number — dark, cooler regions of intense magnetic activity. During solar minimum very few sunspots appear; solar maximum brings a high concentration, often with more frequent flares. A more active Sun releases a more turbulent stream of particles, which is what ties this cycle to everything else on this dashboard.

aurora.title: Aurora Forecast
aurora.subtitle: Where the aurora is likely to be visible overhead in the next hour, on both hemispheres.

about.title: About the aurora forecast
about.body: Aurora happens when charged particles from the solar wind are funnelled down Earth's magnetic field lines and collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, making them glow — green from oxygen at around 100–300 km, red higher up, and blue or purple from nitrogen. Because the particles follow the magnetic field, the display forms an oval centred on each magnetic pole rather than a cap over the geographic ones, and the two hemispheres light up near-simultaneously.

about.title: How to read the globe
about.body: This is NOAA's OVATION model, which estimates the percentage chance of seeing aurora directly overhead over the next 30 to 90 minutes. It is driven by solar wind measured at L1, roughly a million miles upstream, which is what buys the forecast its short lead time. Colour and height both track that probability: low chances sit close to the surface in green, stronger ones rise and shift through yellow to red. A quiet forecast showing only thin polar ovals is the normal state — the ovals widen and push toward the equator as geomagnetic activity increases, which is the same disturbance the Kp and Dst pages measure.
